concept.name: In-the-money option
concept.definition: An in-the-money (ITM) option is an option with positive intrinsic value: a call whose strike is below the current underlying price, or a put whose strike is above it. Its premium equals intrinsic value plus any remaining time value.
concept.intuition: An ITM option is already 'winning' — exercising it immediately would capture real value, so most of its price moves one-for-one with the underlying.
concept.mechanics: Intrinsic value = max(S - K, 0) for calls and max(K - S, 0) for puts. ITM options have deltas approaching +1 (calls) or -1 (puts) and are the ones exercised (or automatically exercised) at expiration.
concept.formula: Intrinsic value: call = max(S - K, 0); put = max(K - S, 0). Total premium = intrinsic value + time value.
concept.failure_modes: Deep ITM options are illiquid and wide bid-ask spreads can erode the apparent value; holders of ITM American options also carry early-assignment and dividend considerations. Time value can be negative for deep ITM European puts under discounting.
concept.misconceptions: Being ITM does not mean the trade is profitable — an option bought for $8 that is now $5 ITM is still a losing position. ITM short options can be assigned at any time (American style), not only at expiration.
concept.example: With stock at $55, the $50 call is $5 in-the-money; if it trades at $6.20, then $5 is intrinsic value and $1.20 is time value.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
